newsitem.title: USA: Tell McVeigh he must die, U.S. bomb jury urged.
newsitem.headline: Tell McVeigh he must die, U.S. bomb jury urged.

text.p: A prosecutor pleaded with jurors on Thursday to look into the eyes of convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh and tell him he was a traitor who deserved to die.

"Look into the eyes of a coward and tell him you will have courage," prosecutor Beth Wilkinson said in a final appeal to the jury that will decide whether McVeigh should be put to death or spend the rest of his life in prison for bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people.
"Tell him he is no patriot. He is a traitor and he deserves to die," she said. "It's time, it's time for justice."

After a closing argument by the defence, which will appeal to the jury to spare McVeigh's life, and instructions on the law from federal Judge Richard Matsch, the jury was expected on Thursday to begin its deliberations on McVeigh's fate.

In her solemn 35-minute statement to the hushed courtroom, Wilkinson stressed the enormity of McVeigh's crime, saying the April 19, 1995 attack was "the most bloody domestic terrorist act in the history of our country."

Wilkinson said McVeigh, a 29-year-old ex-soldier, killed more Americans on a single day than were killed in combat in the Gulf War. "There would not be enough seats in this courtroom if we could bring them all back today," she said.

"We never knew such a dark and horrible place existed in America until Timothy McVeigh sent us there," she said. "It is time for justice, it is time to impose the ultimate sanction on the man responsible for this terror ... Sentence Timothy McVeigh to death."

Wilkinson said McVeigh "believed he could take the law into his own hands and declare war on his fellow Americans." He believed it was his right "to murder innocent men, women and children" and "carried out a daytime assault to insure maximum carnage," she said.
Wilkinson said she knew the jurors' task was difficult. "Weighing the worth of anyone's life is a gut-wrenching task," she said.
McVeigh was found guilty on June 2 of 11 murder, conspiracy and bombing charges, all of which carried a possible death penalty.

During the penalty phase of the trial that began last week, the prosecution called dozens of survivors, bomb victims and rescue workers -- many in tears -- to testify about the horror of the bombing and the physical and emotional scars it left.

The defence called relatives, friends and former neighbours of McVeigh who said he was a cheerful child, a good student and a model soldier. The most poignant moment came on Wednesday when his parents pleaded for his life.

The defence said McVeigh was deeply disturbed by the deaths of about 80 Branch Davidian cult members in the 1993 federal siege of their compound in Waco, Texas. The government said McVeigh bombed the Murrah building on the second anniversary of the end of the Waco siege to avenge the deaths.

Wilkinson listed the aggravating circumstances she said the jury should consider in deciding between life and death. They included McVeigh's meticulous planning of the attack, the deaths of eight federal agents and the serious physical and emotional damage inflicted on victims.

She scoffed at the mitigating factors the defence said should persuade the jury to have mercy. McVeigh's lack of a criminal record before the bombing was "a mere pebble compared to the pounds of death and destruction that Mr. McVeigh caused," she said.

McVeigh's beliefs about Waco were "a misguided fantasy, not a reality" and the jury should dismiss McVeigh's attempt to blame the government for his crime, Wilkinson said. Several of the babies killed in the Murrah building were not even born when Waco happened, she said.
